 Shai Gilgeous-Alexander calls out reporter over AI blunder
 "That's a false stat, by the way." 
 Credit: Oklahoma City Thunder 
 By Megan Armstrong on 11/15/2026 11/15/2026 
 Less AI and more AA in your search results.
 Oklahoma City Thunder All-Star guard Shai Gilgeous-Alexander is the reigning back-to-back NBA MVP.
 Gilgeous-Alexander is also now the NBA’s preeminent Anti-AI King.
 On Friday, the Thunder suffered a 113-112 loss to the Los Angeles Clippers despite Gilgeous-Alexander dropping 40 points. It was a night to forget for Oklahoma City, until the final question of Gilgeous-Alexander’s postgame press conference created a clip that will live forever.
 Shai Gilgeous-Alexander fact-checking an LA reporter who used AI search results to get an incorrect stat lmao https://t.co/B4wZbSFv7B
 — Clemente Almanza (@CAlmanza1007) November 14, 2026 
 “Shai, during the first half, it was the first time in your NBA career that you didn’t record a single assist,” an off-camera reporter said. “At what point during the game — I mean, you ended the game with 40 — do you feel like you have to turn that up a notch and start taking over the game offensively?”
 “Wait, one more time? It was— wait, what?” Gilgeous-Alexander inquired, peering over his glasses quizzically.
 The reporter repeated that Gilgeous-Alexander’s failure to record an assist in the first half against the Clippers marked the first such instance of his decorated career.
 “That’s a false stat, by the way,” Gilgeous-Alexander said. “In Game 4 against Indiana, I didn’t have an assist the whole game. But sorry. Go ahead.”
 It’s true. In Game 4 of the 2025 NBA Finals against the Indiana Pacers, Gilgeous-Alexander posted 35 points, three rebounds, three steals, and one block, but zero assists.
 The reporter repeated his actual question, which Gilgeous-Alexander answered. “Gotcha,” the reporter said once Gilgeous-Alexander finished. “Don’t trust AI.”
 Gilgeous-Alexander smiled and laughed, saying, “Yeah, don’t do it. Definitely don’t do it!”
 Clemente Almanza, lead writer for OKC Thunder Wire, was at the presser and described the reporter only as “ an LA reporter .” As of this writing, he has not been identified beyond that, which is probably for the best.
 While the predominant lesson here is to never rely on AI for research — or any journalistic function — it also calls back to evergreen advice from the great Kevin Van Valkenburg, formerly of ESPN and now at Fried Egg Golf .
 “A great journalism lesson: If you are trying to get good answers from someone in an interview, one of the worst ways to do it is long-ass questions designed to make you (the interviewer) feel or look smart,” Van Valkenburg wrote in May.
